records.name: Jeju
records.current_summary: No region-specific law, incident or enforcement finding about trans people exists in the audited record for this island, and the national framework applies: trans status is not criminalised; a May 2024 ruling removed surgical requirements for changing registered sex; and the July 2024 damages judgment against police advice that a transitioning person avoid public restrooms — with its appellate language on restroom use as a fundamental and universal human right — governs here as in the rest of the country. The same sources' national survey data (2021: large majorities of trans respondents reporting fear-driven facility avoidance) and a 2021 damages award for a student barred from academy restrooms describe the practical baseline.  An earlier characterisation of this island as the country's most permissive region was a model prior, not a finding; it is not supported by any surviving audited source and has been removed. What the record can support for a visitor is the national position on this island — lawful status, available courts, social ambivalence about facilities — and no locally documented fact making this island safer or harsher than that picture.

sources.claim: Korea Times (22 July 2024): the Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal and finalised a 300,000 won damages award (against a 3 million won claim) ruling that police advice to a person transitioning from male to female, who had obtained court approval for a family-register gender change in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms infringed personal rights; the appellate court held that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right. The article also reports a 2021 NHRCK survey of 591 transgender respondents, 41% of whom reported avoiding facilities out of fear. This is the national framework this island division is scored against; the article contains no Jeju-specific incident.

Yonhap wire (8 May 2024): a regional court in Yeongdong approved changing the registered sex from male to female for five transgender applicants without sex-reassignment surgery, holding that it is against the law to condition gender change on surgery, and that court guidelines requiring surgery are now mere reference, not criteria; the court said every human being has the right to form their character and live a life according to their gender identity. This national ruling removed the surgical prerequisite for registered-sex change and is the framework this island division is scored against; the wire contains no Jeju-specific content.

records.name: Tacna
records.current_summary: On 19 April 2025 Marcia Paucara Cora, a 48-year-old trans woman, was found dead in a room of a hostel in central Tacna; the autopsy recorded death by mechanical asphyxia through compression of the upper airways. She had entered with a man who registered under a false identity and left alone roughly two hours later; police hold camera footage and taxi-driver testimony but, per the audited reporting, had not identified the suspect, and the case was being investigated as a possible hate crime. On 23 May her family and local LGBT collectives held a vigil describing the killing as the reflection of a structural system of violence.  The framework that reaches a visitor in Tacna in full: the audited reporting records that this country has neither a gender-identity law nor a hate-crime statute — so anti-trans violence can only be prosecuted as ordinary homicide, and the 'hate crime' label marks investigative posture, not a charge — and that a recently promulgated national law restricts public-bathroom access by reference to sexual orientation. Beyond this one incident and its response, no local ordinance, policing pattern against trans people, or municipal protection is documented; the investigating-as-hate-crime posture within a statute-less system is the audited local reality.

Her family and local LGTBIQ+ collectives held a vigil on Friday 23 May demanding justice, describing the killing as the reflection of a structural system of violence that silences trans lives. The body was discovered by hostel staff when the rental time expired; no suspect had been identified in the audited text.

records.name: Caldas
records.current_summary: No Caldas-specific law, enforcement practice or incident finding for trans people appears in the record's surviving sources. The national reporting they carry frames what a visitor stands under anywhere in the country: an English-language international paper (April 2025) reported the killing of Sara Millerey, a trans woman beaten in daylight and filmed by onlookers in a northern metropolitan area, whose death from her injuries provoked national alarm over transfemicide; and an international daily's investigation (July 2024) documented armed groups in a southern department circulating 'social cleansing' flyers against trans women and forcing them from their homes, with dozens killed nationally.  Those reported cases concern other departments. Nothing here marks Caldas as materially safer or more dangerous than that national picture, and because such violence surfaces where monitors and journalists can reach, the absence of Caldas-specific findings is weak evidence of safety, not proof of it.

sources.claim: El País English edition (14 April 2025) reports Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman beaten in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, filmed by onlookers and thrown into a creek, who died of a second cardiac arrest the following afternoon with no one arrested; the article states hate crimes killed 13 trans people in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025 and that her death provoked national outrage and mobilisations against transphobia. That national transfemicide alarm is the picture this department is assessed against; the report contains no Caldas-specific information.

The Guardian investigation (30 July 2024) documents armed groups in Caquetá giving trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed and circulating 'social cleansing' flyers against trans women, quotes an activist saying the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide (recording the killings as ordinary cases), and reports 41 trans women killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024. This national armed-group violence and displacement baseline is what this department is assessed against; the report contains no Caldas-specific information.

Wikipedia's 'LGBTQ rights in Colombia' page states the national framework a visitor stands under in Cundinamarca: since 1993 a person may change the gender marker on their Colombian birth certificate, with current options F, M, NB (no binario) and T (transgénero). On 9 July 2026 outgoing justice minister Jorge Iván Cuervo signed Decree 0732 of 2026, which obliges public notaries to complete the request within five business days, makes the first request (and a simultaneous name change) free of charge, and shields the change history from public disclosure. The Constitutional Court's 4 February 2022 ruling ordered the government to offer the nonbinary ('NB') option to everyone and to ask Congress to amend the relevant laws, and since August 2023 passports issued within Colombia offer three gender options (male, female, X). A 2016 report (Cartografía de derechos trans en Colombia, by OutRight Action International, El Aquelarre Trans and PAIIS) documented notaries refusing to process name changes and recommended ending the psychiatric pathologisation of transgender identity. Gender-marker change is a notarial/bureaucratic process with no surgery or court ruling required and applies equally in Cundinamarca.
